headline: High risk of shared-filesystem prompt injection and capability conflict; default cross-agent file exchange can also cascade errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write the filesystem and use MCP, and their shared state is explicitly via filesystem/git for agent_a while agent_b warns about separate roots to avoid overwriting session files. That creates a plausible default bridge for one agent to ingest the other's content as instructions, though not a guaranteed hijack.
conditions: IF either agent reads files produced by the other without provenance checks
IF both agents share the same workspace or root directory
mitigations: Separate working roots for each agent
Disable automatic ingestion of peer-generated files
Add provenance tags to shared artifacts
Review any file-based handoff before execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches source code, git history, shell environment, and files in cwd; agent_b touches session summaries, learned skills, hooks, agent definitions, and security findings. Because both have filesystem access and agent_a has broad network egress while agent_b can call external APIs, sensitive workspace data can flow into outputs or remote services in default setups.
conditions: IF either agent is pointed at a workspace containing secrets or regulated data
IF either agent forwards file contents or session summaries to external APIs
mitigations: Use a scrubbed test workspace
Remove secrets from cwd before running
Restrict outbound network/API access
Set separate storage roots for session artifacts
Audit generated outputs for sensitive strings

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, git-state modification, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and MCP use. Their shared-state model is filesystem/git, so concurrent edits can race and corrupt repo or config state without locking. This is a default-dangerous overlap with potentially irreversible work loss.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or config tree
IF concurrent sessions modify overlapping files without external locking
mitigations: Run only one agent per repo at a time
Use separate clones or worktrees
Pause one agent before the other writes
Commit or stash before handoff
Add file-locking or orchestration locks

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can produce code, shell actions, and git changes that agent_b may then consume through shared files or session artifacts. agent_b's skills/subagents surface suggests it may operationalize prior outputs, so unverified handoff can propagate mistakes. The pathway exists in default file-based workflows, but not enough evidence for high-impact autonomous downstream action.
conditions: IF agent_b treats agent_a-produced files or git diffs as authoritative
IF agent_a's outputs are reused without a verification step
mitigations: Require explicit verification before reuse
Insert a human review gate for handoffs
Pass only summarized, not raw, outputs
Annotate generated artifacts with confidence and source
Re-run checks after each handoff

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not specify a concrete residency or certification mismatch. The only clear compliance-relevant surface is that agent_a handles git credentials and agent_b handles GitHub App/OAuth-related secrets, but no cross-border or regulated-data violation is evidenced. The other agent is cited because the pairwise setup is what could create a mismatch, but the current profiles do not prove one.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into either agent's workspace
IF one agent is deployed under a stricter residency or retention policy than the other
mitigations: Document data classes per agent
Keep regulated data out of both tools
Align retention settings before use
Review OAuth and secret handling scopes
Add a compliance checklist for deployments
